nameStory: The 'black' in black walnut refers to the dark, rich brown heartwood that makes this tree so prized by furniture makers and woodworkers. While the outer bark is actually grayish, the inner wood is so distinctively dark that it earned the tree its common name. Eastern black walnut distinguishes it from other walnut species found elsewhere in North America.
description: Eastern black walnut is a majestic deciduous tree that can tower 50-75 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It's easily recognized by its distinctive compound leaves made up of many leaflets arranged along a central stem, and its famous round nuts enclosed in thick, green hulls. The bark is dark gray with deep furrows, and the tree has an open, spreading branching pattern that creates dappled shade below.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 15-23 pointed leaflets arranged along a central stem, each leaflet 2-4 inches long with serrated edges and a smooth, slightly oily feel

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round nuts about 1.5-2 inches across, encased in thick, yellowish-green hulls that stain your hands dark brown and have a spicy, citrusy smell when crushed

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to blackish bark with deep, diamond-shaped furrows and thick ridges that become more pronounced with age

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Fuzzy, grayish-brown terminal buds that are noticeably larger than side buds, with a woolly texture when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Large tree with an open, broad crown and thick branches that often lean outward, creating an umbrella-like canopy

habitat: In New England, eastern black walnut grows best in rich, moist soils along streams, rivers, and in bottomlands, though it can adapt to well-drained upland sites. You'll often find it in mixed hardwood forests alongside maples, oaks, and hickories, particularly in areas with deep, fertile soil. It prefers full sun to partial shade and is more common in the southern parts of New England.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, often after other trees have leafed out, with small, inconspicuous yellowish-green flowers appearing on dangling catkins in May.
seasonality.summer: Full compound leaves create dense shade, and you can spot the developing green hulled nuts beginning to form by midsummer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and mature nuts fall to the ground in their thick green hulls from September through October.
seasonality.winter: Bare trees show the distinctive diamond-furrowed bark and large, fuzzy terminal buds that help identify the species when leaves are gone.

funFact: Black walnut trees are natural chemical warriors — they release compounds called juglones from their roots, leaves, and hulls that can kill or stunt many other plants growing nearby, essentially creating their own 'dead zones' to reduce competition for nutrients and water.
confusionNotes: Black walnut is most often confused with butternut, but butternut has fewer leaflets per leaf (11-17 vs 15-23) and sticky, fuzzy leaf stems that feel tacky to the touch, while black walnut's leaf stems are smooth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'black' walnut, don't expect to see black bark — the name refers to the dark heartwood inside the tree that's so valuable for furniture making. The nuts you find in grocery stores are usually English or Persian walnuts, not the harder-to-crack but more flavorful black walnuts.
compareHints: Compared to butternut, its closest New England relative, black walnut has more leaflets per compound leaf, smooth (not sticky) leaf stems, and rounder nuts versus butternut's elongated nuts. Black walnut also grows larger and has darker, more deeply furrowed bark, while butternut has lighter gray bark with flatter ridges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the walnut family members in New England, butternut is easily distinguished from black walnut by its pale gray bark and oblong, sticky-husked nuts versus black walnut's dark bark and round nuts.
Persian walnut differs from our native black walnut and butternut by having smooth-edged leaflets (not serrated), lighter gray bark, and round nuts (butternut has oblong nuts).
Japanese walnut differs from our native black walnut in having a generally more northern cold tolerance and different nut characteristics.
